steps.steering_note: The candidate recognizes backward induction and record-only choices but made a consequential state-dependent continuation-value error, so this question isolates that issue in a harder three-remaining-draw continuation problem.

steps.title: Selecting the Fourth-Best from a Sample
steps.prompt:
A uniformly random permutation of 12 distinct items is presented. You observe the first 5 items, but learn only their complete relative ordering (so you know which is largest, second-largest, and so on among those 5, but not their ranks among all 12). You must then select exactly one of these 5 items. You win if your selected item is the fourth-largest of all 12 items.

Determine the maximum possible probability of winning as an exact fraction, and give an optimal rule. Prove that no rule that depends on the entire observed relative-order pattern, including the order in which the 5 items appeared, can do better.
steps.reference:
Call global rank 1 the largest item, global rank 2 the second-largest, and so forth. The desired item has global rank 4.

An optimal rule is: select the second-largest among the first 5 observed items.

To evaluate this, condition on any particular complete relative-order pattern of the first 5 positions. Conditional on that pattern, the set S of global ranks appearing in those five positions is still uniformly distributed among all 5-element subsets of {1,2,...,12}. Indeed, for each fixed set S, exactly one assignment of its elements to the five positions realizes the specified relative-order pattern, so every such S has the same conditional probability. Thus the detailed arrival pattern contains no information beyond an item's ordinal rank within the observed sample.

Suppose we select the j-th largest among the first 5 items, where j=1 means the observed maximum. For this selected item to be global rank 4:

- Exactly j-1 of the globally better ranks {1,2,3} must be present in the sample, because those are precisely the observed items above the selected one.
- Global rank 4 itself must be present.
- The remaining 5-j sampled ranks must come from the eight globally worse ranks {5,6,...,12}.

Therefore, for j=1,2,3,4, the conditional success probability is

p_j = [C(3,j-1) C(8,5-j)] / C(12,5).

For j=5 the probability is 0, since four observed items lie above the selected item, whereas a global fourth-largest item has only three items above it in all.

Since C(12,5)=792, the relevant numerators are:

p_1: C(3,0)C(8,4)=70, so p_1=70/792=35/396.
p_2: C(3,1)C(8,3)=3·56=168, so p_2=168/792=7/33.
p_3: C(3,2)C(8,2)=3·28=84, so p_3=84/792=7/66.
p_4: C(3,3)C(8,1)=8, so p_4=8/792=1/99.
p_5=0.

The largest probability is p_2=7/33. Hence selecting the second-largest observed item wins with probability exactly 7/33.

For optimality, fix any full observed relative-order history. As shown above, conditional on that history, selecting the j-th largest observed item has success probability p_j, independent of the particular history. The largest of these is p_2. Thus, at every possible history, selecting the observed second-largest is conditionally optimal. Any deterministic history-dependent rule has conditional success probability at most 7/33 at every history, hence unconditional success probability at most 7/33. Randomization cannot improve this, because it only forms a convex combination of the same conditional action probabilities. Therefore 7/33 is the global optimum.
rubric: Correctly identifies the optimal choice as the second-largest among the five observed items and gives the maximum probability 7/33.
Derives the success probability for each possible observed ordinal choice using correct subset-counting or an equivalent conditional-symmetry argument.
Justifies why the full arrival-order pattern provides no additional useful information and therefore why no adaptive or randomized rule can improve on the stated rule.
steps.answer: None
steps.steering_note: The candidate showed some useful backward-induction structure but made a consequential conditional-continuation error and did not answer Question 3, so this question probes exact conditional symmetry and optimization over history-dependent rules at a more controlled level.

steps.title: Records Conditioned on Their Total
steps.prompt:
A uniformly random permutation of the distinct numbers 1,2,...,8 is revealed from left to right. An entry is called a record if it is larger than every earlier entry; the first entry is therefore always a record. You are told that the permutation has exactly three records in total.

Let M be the position occupied by 8, the overall maximum.

Determine exactly:
1. P(M=8 | the permutation has exactly three records), and
2. E[M | the permutation has exactly three records].

Give a rigorous counting proof. In particular, do not assume that the position of 8 remains uniform after conditioning on the total number of records.
steps.reference:
Let A(n,k) be the number of permutations of {1,...,n} having exactly k left-to-right records.

First compute A(8,3). Insert the new smallest element 1 into a permutation of n-1 elements, after increasing all old labels by 1. If 1 is inserted in the first position, it creates one new record; if it is inserted in any of the other n-1 positions, it creates no new record. Hence

A(n,k) = A(n-1,k-1) + (n-1)A(n-1,k),

with A(1,1)=1 and A(n,k)=0 outside 1<=k<=n.

Using this recurrence, the relevant values A(m,2) are

A(2,2)=1,
A(3,2)=3,
A(4,2)=11,
A(5,2)=50,
A(6,2)=274,
A(7,2)=1764,

and

A(8,3)=13132.

Now count permutations with exactly three records and with 8 at position j. Since 8 is necessarily a record, the first j-1 entries must contain exactly two records. Choose which j-1 elements from {1,...,7} occur before 8, arrange them with exactly two records, and arrange the remaining 8-j elements arbitrarily after 8. Thus the number N_j is

N_j = C(7,j-1) A(j-1,2)(8-j)! = 7! A(j-1,2)/(j-1)!.

This is zero for j=1,2. For j=3,4,5,6,7,8, respectively, the counts are

N_3 = 2520,
N_4 = 2520,
N_5 = 2310,
N_6 = 2100,
N_7 = 1918,
N_8 = 1764.

They sum to

2520+2520+2310+2100+1918+1764 = 13132,

as required.

Therefore

P(M=8 | exactly three records) = N_8/A(8,3) = 1764/13132 = 441/3283.

For the conditional expectation,

E[M | exactly three records]
= (3N_3+4N_4+5N_5+6N_6+7N_7+8N_8)/13132
= (3(2520)+4(2520)+5(2310)+6(2100)+7(1918)+8(1764))/13132
= 69328/13132
= 17332/3283.

Hence the exact answers are

P(M=8 | exactly three records) = 441/3283,

E[M | exactly three records] = 17332/3283.

The conditioning strongly biases the maximum away from the final position: it is not valid to use the unconditional probability 1/8.
rubric: Correctly derives or otherwise rigorously justifies the record-count recurrence A(n,k)=A(n-1,k-1)+(n-1)A(n-1,k), including the denominator A(8,3)=13132.
Correctly counts permutations with maximum 8 at each position j by requiring exactly two records before it, obtaining the relevant conditional counts or an equivalent valid formula.
Obtains both exact final results 441/3283 and 17332/3283, with a valid conditional-probability and expectation calculation.
steps.answer: None
steps.steering_note: The candidate handled a discrete optimal-stopping dynamic program well but made a consequential conditional-case error in a continuous one, so this probes exact conditional counting and recurrence reasoning without relying on optimization heuristics.

verdict.assessment: The candidate solved Q1 correctly, including the exact value and essentially valid dynamic-programming optimality argument. Q2 showed strong backward-induction structure and got the stage-2 rule right, but made a consequential error for x1>=1/2: the continuation value omitted the integral over x2 in [x1,1], replacing it with a constant 3/8. This led to an incorrect first threshold (3/4 instead of (1+sqrt(6))/5) and incorrect optimum (67/96). Q3-Q5 were unanswered, so there is no evidence on the harder conditional-record counting or four-draw value-function tasks. Overall this demonstrates capable reasoning on a standard secretary problem but insufficient reliability and coverage for a higher rating.

steps.title: Square Roots of Doubling
steps.prompt:
Determine and prove a complete classification of all functions f: Z_{>0} -> Z_{>0} satisfying

f(f(n)) = 2n

for every positive integer n. Your answer must state exactly how every such function can be constructed, and prove both that every solution has your form and that every function of your stated form is a solution.
steps.reference:
Let O be the set of positive odd integers. All solutions are obtained as follows.

Choose a fixed-point-free involution h: O -> O; equivalently, partition O into unordered pairs. For each pair {u,v}, choose an orientation, encoded by a function a: O -> {0,1}, such that

h(h(m)) = m,  h(m) != m,  and  a(m) + a(h(m)) = 1

for every odd m. Define, for k >= 0 and m odd,

f(2^k m) = 2^(k+a(m)) h(m).

This is the complete classification.

Necessity:
From f(f(n))=2n, apply f to both sides to get

f(f(f(n))) = f(2n).

Applying the original equation with input f(n) gives

f(f(f(n))) = 2f(n).

Therefore f(2n)=2f(n) for every n. By induction,

f(2^k m)=2^k f(m)

for every k>=0 and odd m.

Now fix odd m. Write f(m) uniquely as

f(m)=2^{a(m)}h(m),

where a(m)>=0 and h(m) is odd. Using the doubling relation,

f(f(m)) = f(2^{a(m)}h(m)) = 2^{a(m)}f(h(m))
=2^{a(m)+a(h(m))}h(h(m)).

But f(f(m))=2m. Since m and h(h(m)) are odd, uniqueness of the decomposition into a power of 2 times an odd integer yields

h(h(m))=m
and
a(m)+a(h(m))=1.

Because both exponents are nonnegative integers, each is either 0 or 1. Also h(m)=m would imply 2a(m)=1, impossible. Thus h is a fixed-point-free involution on the odd positive integers, and a assigns opposite values 0 and 1 to the two elements of every h-pair. The displayed formula for f then follows from f(2^k m)=2^k f(m).

Sufficiency:
Conversely, choose h and a with the stated properties and define f(2^k m)=2^(k+a(m))h(m). Every positive integer has a unique representation 2^k m with m odd, so this defines f unambiguously. Then

f(f(2^k m))
= f(2^(k+a(m))h(m))
= 2^(k+a(m)+a(h(m)))h(h(m))
= 2^(k+1)m
= 2(2^k m).

Hence f(f(n))=2n for every positive integer n.

For example, one may pair consecutive odd numbers (1,3), (5,7), ...; set a to be 0 on the smaller member and 1 on the larger member; then extend using the formula above.
rubric: Derives the key identity f(2n)=2f(n) and correctly extends it to f(2^k m)=2^k f(m).
Correctly decomposes the action on odd integers into a fixed-point-free involution h and complementary exponents a in {0,1}, proving these conditions are necessary.
States a complete construction and verifies directly that every constructed function satisfies f(f(n))=2n.
steps.answer:
We classify all functions
\[
f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to \mathbb Z_{>0}
\]
such that
\[
f(f(n))=2n\qquad(\forall n\ge 1).
\]

The answer is:

> Such a function exists, and every such function is obtained by choosing a partition of the positive integers into disjoint infinite “chains”
> \[
> a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots
> \]
> satisfying
> \[
> a_{k+2}=2a_k\qquad(\forall k\ge 0),
> \]
> and then defining
> \[
> f(a_k)=a_{k+1}\qquad(\forall k\ge 0).
> \]
> Equivalently, each chain is determined by a pair of positive odd integers \((u,v)\), and has the form
> \[
> u,\ v,\ 2u,\ 2v,\ 4u,\ 4v,\ 8u,\ 8v,\dots
> \]
> and \(f\) sends each term to the next one:
> \[
> f(2^m u)=2^m v,\qquad f(2^m v)=2^{m+1}u\qquad(m\ge 0).
> \]
> The set of all positive integers must be partitioned into such disjoint chains.

We now prove this completely.

---

## 1. First basic consequences

Assume
\[
f(f(n))=2n\qquad(\forall n\ge 1).
\]

We first derive some necessary properties.

### Lemma 1: \(f\) is injective.

If \(f(a)=f(b)\), then applying \(f\) to both sides gives
\[
f(f(a))=f(f(b)).
\]
Hence
\[
2a=2b,
\]
so \(a=b\). Thus \(f\) is injective.

---

### Lemma 2: No odd number lies in the image of \(f\) twice, and the iterates of any \(n\) are all distinct.

If \(f^i(n)=f^j(n)\) with \(i<j\), then by injectivity we could cancel \(f^i\) and get
\[
n=f^{j-i}(n).
\]
If \(j-i=2t\), then
\[
f^{2t}(n)=2^t n,
\]
so \(2^t n=n\), impossible for \(t>0\).  
If \(j-i=2t+1\), then applying \(f\),
\[
f^{2t+2}(n)=f(n),
\]
so
\[
2^{t+1}n=f(n).
\]
Applying \(f\) again gives
\[
2^{t+1}f(n)=2n,
\]
hence \(f(n)=2^{-t}n\), impossible unless \(t=0\), which would say \(f(n)=n\), but then \(n=f(f(n))=2n\), impossible.

So the forward orbit
\[
n,\ f(n),\ f^2(n)=2n,\ f^3(n)=f(2n),\ f^4(n)=4n,\dots
\]
has no repetitions.

---

### Lemma 3: For every \(n\),
\[
f(2n)=2f(n).
\]

This is very important.

Indeed,
\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(2n).
\]
But also
\[
f(f(f(n)))=2f(n),
\]
because applying the identity with input \(f(n)\) gives
\[
f(f(f(n)))=2f(n).
\]
Hence
\[
f(2n)=2f(n)\qquad(\forall n).
\]

By induction,
\[
f(2^k n)=2^k f(n)\qquad(\forall k\ge 0).
\]

So \(f\) commutes with doubling.

---

## 2. Reduction to odd numbers

Every positive integer has a unique form
\[
n=2^k m
\]
with \(m\) odd.

By Lemma 3,
\[
f(n)=f(2^k m)=2^k f(m).
\]
Thus the whole function is completely determined by its values on odd numbers.

Now if \(m\) is odd, then
\[
f(f(m))=2m
\]
is even, so \(f(m)\) cannot be even/odd arbitrarily. Let us analyze its 2-adic valuation.

Write
\[
f(m)=2^r t
\]
with \(t\) odd. Then
\[
2m=f(f(m))=f(2^r t)=2^r f(t).
\]
Hence
\[
f(t)=2^{1-r}m.
\]
Since \(f(t)\) is a positive integer, we must have \(1-r\ge 0\), so \(r\le 1\). Thus \(r=0\) or \(r=1\).

But \(r=0\) would mean \(f(m)\) is odd. Then \(f(f(m))\) would be \(f(\text{odd})\), and from the equation it equals \(2m\), an even number. That is possible in principle, but let us check what it means: if \(f(m)=t\) is odd, then
\[
f(t)=2m.
\]
So odd numbers can map to odd numbers, but then the next odd maps to an even number. The right way to organize this is by pairing odd numbers.

The key observation is this:

### Lemma 4: If \(u\) is odd and \(f(u)=2^r v\) with \(v\) odd, then \(r\in\{0,1\}\), and:
- if \(r=0\), then \(f(v)=2u\);
- if \(r=1\), then \(f(v)=u\).

This follows exactly from
\[
2u=f(f(u))=f(2^r v)=2^r f(v).
\]

So on odd numbers, \(f\) links odd numbers in pairs.

---

## 3. The odd-number graph

Let \(O\) be the set of positive odd integers.

For each odd \(u\), write
\[
f(u)=2^{\varepsilon(u)}\phi(u),
\]
where \(\phi(u)\in O\) and \(\varepsilon(u)\in\{0,1\}\).

Then from Lemma 4:
- if \(\varepsilon(u)=0\), then \(\varepsilon(\phi(u))=1\) and \(\phi(\phi(u))=u\);
- if \(\varepsilon(u)=1\), then \(\varepsilon(\phi(u))=0\) and \(\phi(\phi(u))=u\).

So \(\phi:O\to O\) is an involution with no fixed points, and \(\varepsilon\) alternates between 0 and 1 on each 2-cycle.

That means the odd numbers are partitioned into unordered pairs
\[
\{u,v\}
\]
of distinct odd numbers, and for each pair exactly one of the two orientations occurs:
\[
f(u)=v,\quad f(v)=2u,
\]
or equivalently
\[
f(v)=u,\quad f(u)=2v.
\]

Once this is chosen for odd numbers, Lemma 3 forces all values on even numbers:
\[
f(2^m u)=2^m f(u),\qquad f(2^m v)=2^m f(v).
\]

Thus if on an odd pair \(\{u,v\}\) we choose
\[
f(u)=v,\qquad f(v)=2u,
\]
then for all \(m\ge 0\),
\[
f(2^m u)=2^m v,\qquad f(2^m v)=2^{m+1}u.
\]

This gives precisely the chain
\[
u,\ v,\ 2u,\ 2v,\ 4u,\ 4v,\dots
\]
with \(f\) sending each term to the next.

Because every positive integer is uniquely \(2^m\) times an odd integer, and the odd integers are partitioned into pairs, these chains are disjoint and cover all positive integers.

So every solution must have the announced form.

---

## 4. Construction of all solutions

Now we state the classification cleanly.

Choose a partition of the set of positive odd integers into disjoint 2-element sets
\[
\{u_i,v_i\}\qquad(i\in I),
\]
where \(u_i,v_i\) are distinct odd integers.

For each pair \(\{u_i,v_i\}\), choose one of the two orientations; say we choose
\[
f(u_i)=v_i,\qquad f(v_i)=2u_i.
\]
Then define for all \(m\ge 0\):
\[
f(2^m u_i)=2^m v_i,\qquad f(2^m v_i)=2^{m+1}u_i.
\]

Since every positive integer belongs to exactly one set of the form \(\{2^m u_i,2^m v_i:m\ge 0\}\), this defines \(f\) on all of \(\mathbb Z_{>0}\).

This is equivalent to saying that \(\mathbb Z_{>0}\) is partitioned into chains
\[
u_i,\ v_i,\ 2u_i,\ 2v_i,\ 4u_i,\ 4v_i,\dots
\]
and \(f\) is the successor map along each chain.

---

## 5. Verification that every such construction works

Take one chain
\[
u,\ v,\ 2u,\ 2v,\ 4u,\ 4v,\dots
\]
with \(u,v\) odd, and define
\[
f(2^m u)=2^m v,\qquad f(2^m v)=2^{m+1}u.
\]

Then for every \(m\ge 0\),
\[
f(f(2^m u))=f(2^m v)=2^{m+1}u=2(2^m u),
\]
and
\[
f(f(2^m v))=f(2^{m+1}u)=2^{m+1}v=2(2^m v).
\]

So on that chain,
\[
f(f(n))=2n.
\]
Since the chains are disjoint and cover all positive integers, the identity holds for every \(n\).

Thus every function of the stated form is indeed a solution.

---

## 6. Final classification

We can now summarize the complete classification.

## Theorem
A function \(f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}\) satisfies
\[
f(f(n))=2n\qquad(\forall n\ge 1)
\]
if and only if the set of positive odd integers is partitioned into disjoint pairs
\[
\{u_i,v_i\},
\]
and for each pair one chooses one of the two orientations
\[
f(u_i)=v_i,\quad f(v_i)=2u_i
\]
or
\[
f(v_i)=u_i,\quad f(u_i)=2v_i.
\]
Then \(f\) is extended to all positive integers by
\[
f(2^m x)=2^m f(x)\qquad(m\ge 0,\ x\text{ odd}).
\]

Equivalently, \(\mathbb Z_{>0}\) is partitioned into disjoint chains
\[
u_i,\ v_i,\ 2u_i,\ 2v_i,\ 4u_i,\ 4v_i,\dots
\]
with \(u_i,v_i\) odd, and \(f\) maps each term to the next term of its chain.

This describes exactly all solutions.
steps.steering_note: With no prior evidence, this structural functional-equation problem probes algebraic manipulation, valuation reasoning, and the ability to give a necessary-and-sufficient classification.

steps.title: A Vieta-jumping divisibility theorem
steps.prompt:
Let a and b be positive integers such that

(ab+1) divides (a^2+b^2).

Prove that the integer

k = (a^2+b^2)/(ab+1)

is a perfect square.

Your proof must be self-contained; in particular, justify every descent step and handle all exceptional cases.
steps.reference:
Let

k = (a^2+b^2)/(ab+1),

so that

a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1).   (1)

We prove that k is a square. Suppose, for contradiction, that there is a solution in positive integers a,b for which k is not a square. Fix this k and choose a solution (a,b) with a+b minimal. By symmetry, assume a >= b.

First, k cannot equal 1, since 1 is a square. Hence k >= 2.

We establish an exceptional-case lemma. Suppose k >= b^2. Reducing (1) modulo a gives

b^2 ≡ k (mod a).

Therefore k-b^2 = ta for some integer t >= 0. Substitute k=b^2+ta into (1):

a^2+b^2 = (b^2+ta)(ab+1)
          = ab^3+b^2+ta^2b+ta.

After subtracting b^2 and dividing by a>0, this becomes

a = b^3+tab+t.   (2)

If t>=1, then the right side of (2) is strictly greater than a, because tab >= a (as t,b>=1), and b^3+t>0. This is impossible. Thus t=0. Equation (2) then gives a=b^3, while k=b^2. Hence k is a square. Consequently, under our contrary assumption that k is not a square, we must have

k < b^2.   (3)

Now regard (1) as a quadratic equation in a:

X^2-kbX+(b^2-k)=0.   (4)

One integer root is X=a. Since the coefficients are integers, the other root is

a' = kb-a,

which is also an integer. By the product-of-roots relation,

aa' = b^2-k.

By (3), b^2-k>0, so a'>0.

We next show a'<b. Let

P(X)=X^2-kbX+(b^2-k).

Then P(a)=0 and

P(b) = b^2-kb^2+b^2-k = (2-k)b^2-k < 0,

because k>=2. Since P is an upward-opening quadratic and P(b)<0, the number b lies strictly between its two real roots. One root is a, and a>=b. In fact a>b because P(b) is not zero. Therefore the other root satisfies

0<a'<b.

Since a' is the other root of (4), it satisfies

(a')^2-kba'+(b^2-k)=0,

which rearranges to

(a')^2+b^2 = k(a'b+1).

Thus (a',b) is another positive-integer solution for the same k. But a'<b<=a, so

a'+b < a+b,

contradicting the minimal choice of (a,b).

This contradiction shows that no nonsquare k can occur. Therefore

(a^2+b^2)/(ab+1)

is always a perfect square.
rubric: Introduces k and correctly converts the divisibility hypothesis into a^2+b^2=k(ab+1), then sets up a minimal-counterexample argument for a fixed nonsquare k.
Correctly handles the crucial case k>=b^2, using the congruence k≡b^2 (mod a) to prove that this case forces k=b^2, hence is already square.
Uses the quadratic in a to construct the second positive integer root a'=kb-a, proves 0<a'<b, verifies that (a',b) is another solution for the same k, and obtains the descent contradiction.
steps.answer:
We will prove:

> If \(a,b\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\) and
> \[
> ab+1 \mid a^2+b^2,
> \]
> then
> \[
> k=\frac{a^2+b^2}{ab+1}
> \]
> is a perfect square.

The standard way is a descent argument (Vieta jumping). I will make every step explicit.

---

## 1. Rewrite the condition

Since \(ab+1\mid a^2+b^2\), there exists a positive integer \(k\) such that
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1).
\]
We must prove that \(k\) is a square.

We argue by contradiction.

Assume there exists a pair \((a,b)\) of positive integers for which
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1)
\]
and \(k\) is **not** a perfect square.

Among all such counterexamples, choose one with \(a+b\) minimal. By symmetry in \(a,b\), we may assume
\[
a\ge b.
\]

We will derive a smaller counterexample, contradiction.

---

## 2. First easy case: \(a=b\)

If \(a=b\), then
\[
2a^2 = k(a^2+1).
\]
Hence
\[
k=\frac{2a^2}{a^2+1}.
\]
Since \(a^2+1>a^2\), we have
\[
0<k<2.
\]
But \(k\) is a positive integer, so \(k=1\).

Then
\[
2a^2=a^2+1 \implies a^2=1 \implies a=1.
\]
Thus \(k=1\), which is a perfect square.

So in any counterexample we must have
\[
a>b.
\]

---

## 3. View the equation as a quadratic in \(a\)

From
\[
a^2+b^2 = kab + k
\]
we get
\[
a^2-kba+(b^2-k)=0.
\]
So \(a\) is an integer root of the quadratic
\[
x^2-kbx+(b^2-k)=0.
\]
By Vieta’s formulas, the other root is
\[
a' = kb-a.
\]
Also
\[
a+a'=kb,\qquad aa'=b^2-k.
\]

Since the polynomial has integer coefficients and one integer root \(a\), the other root \(a'\) is also an integer.

We now show that \(a'\) is a positive integer smaller than \(a\). This will produce descent.

---

## 4. Show \(a'>0\)

Suppose \(a'\le 0\). Since \(a' = kb-a\), this means
\[
a\ge kb.
\]
Using the defining equation,
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1)\le a^2+\frac{a^2}{k}+? 
\]
That route is awkward; let us argue directly.

From \(a\ge kb\), we get
\[
a^2 \ge kab.
\]
Hence
\[
a^2+b^2 = kab+k \le a^2 + k.
\]
Therefore
\[
b^2 \le k.
\]
But from \(aa'=b^2-k\) and \(a'\le 0\), we have
\[
b^2-k = aa' \le 0,
\]
so again \(b^2\le k\).

Now compare with the quadratic relation:
\[
a^2-kba+b^2-k=0.
\]
If \(a\ge kb\), then
\[
a^2-kba = a(a-kb)\ge 0.
\]
Thus
\[
0=a^2-kba+b^2-k \ge b^2-k.
\]
So indeed \(b^2\le k\).

If \(b^2<k\), then \(aa'=b^2-k<0\), so \(a'<0\). That is compatible so far. We need a contradiction another way.

Use
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1).
\]
Since \(a\ge kb\),
\[
a^2+b^2 \ge kba + b^2.
\]
Thus
\[
k(ab+1)=a^2+b^2 \ge kab+b^2,
\]
hence
\[
k\ge b^2.
\]
So in fact we again get \(k\ge b^2\).

If \(k=b^2\), then from \(aa'=b^2-k\) we get \(aa'=0\), so \(a'=0\), hence \(a=kb=b^3\). Plugging into
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1)=b^2(ab+1)
\]
gives
\[
b^6+b^2=b^2(b^4+1)=b^6+b^2,
\]
which is true. But then
\[
k=b^2
\]
is a perfect square, contrary to the assumption that \(k\) is not a square.

So \(k>b^2\). Then
\[
aa'=b^2-k<0.
\]
Since \(a>0\), this gives \(a'<0\).

Now we exploit minimality. If \(k>b^2\), then from
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1) > b^2(ab+1),
\]
we get
\[
a^2 > ab^3,
\]
so
\[
a>b^3 \ge kb
\]
is not immediate; so this does not help.

A cleaner route is the following standard estimate:

Because \(a>b\),
\[
a^2+b^2 > ab+1,
\]
so \(k\ge 1\). If \(k=1\), then
\[
a^2+b^2=ab+1.
\]
But for \(a>b\ge1\),
\[
a^2+b^2-ab = \left(a-\frac b2\right)^2+\frac{3b^2}{4} \ge 1,
\]
so equality forces a tiny case; checking gives only \(a=b=1\), impossible since \(a>b\). Hence \(k\ge2\).

Now if \(a'\le0\), then
\[
a\ge kb\ge 2b.
\]
Therefore
\[
a^2+b^2 \ge 4b^2+b^2=5b^2.
\]
But
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1)\le \frac{a}{b}(ab+1)\cdot ? 
\]
This is again not efficient.

Let us instead use the identity
\[
a'=\frac{b^2-k}{a}.
\]
Indeed \(aa'=b^2-k\). If \(a'\le0\), then \(b^2-k\le0\), so \(k\ge b^2\). If \(k=b^2\), then \(k\) is a square, impossible. Hence \(k>b^2\).

But then
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1) > b^2ab+b^2 = b^2(a b+1),
\]
so dividing by \(b>0\),
\[
\frac{a^2}{b}+b > ab^2+b.
\]
This simplifies to
\[
a^2 > ab^3,
\]
hence \(a>b^3\). In particular \(a>b\), but we already know that. This still does not contradict.

So let us prove positivity differently, using an upper bound on \(a\).

Since
\[
a^2+b^2 = kab+k,
\]
and \(a>b\), we have
\[
a^2 < a^2+b^2 = kab+k.
\]
Thus
\[
a^2-kab<k,
\]
i.e.
\[
a(a-kb)<k.
\]
If \(a\ge kb\), then the left side is a nonnegative integer. Because \(a-kb\ge0\), if \(a-kb\ge1\), then
\[
a(a-kb)\ge a\ge b+1.
\]
This alone is not enough. But if \(a\ge kb\), then since \(k\ge1\),
\[
a\ge b.
\]
Still not enough.

There is a simpler standard argument:

From Vieta,
\[
a' = kb-a.
\]
Then
\[
a' = \frac{b^2-k}{a}.
\]
Indeed \(aa'=b^2-k\). Since \(a>0\), the sign of \(a'\) is the sign of \(b^2-k\). So it suffices to show
\[
b^2-k>0.
\]

Suppose \(b^2\le k\). Then from
\[
a^2+b^2 = kab+k \ge kab+b^2,
\]
we obtain
\[
a^2\ge kab,
\]
so
\[
a\ge kb
\]
because \(a>0\). Hence
\[
a' = kb-a\le0.
\]
If \(b^2<k\), then \(a'<0\). If \(b^2=k\), then \(a'=0\) and \(k=b^2\) is a square. Therefore in a counterexample \(b^2\neq k\), so necessarily \(b^2<k\), hence \(a'<0\).

Now use the other equation
\[
a+a'=kb.
\]
Since \(a'<0\), we have
\[
a>kb.
\]
Then
\[
a^2+b^2 > kab+b^2.
\]
But \(a^2+b^2=kab+k\), so
\[
kab+k > kab+b^2,
\]
hence
\[
k>b^2.
\]
This is consistent, not contradictory.

So we need a different contradiction. The standard way is to choose the counterexample with minimal \(a\) for fixed \(k\), not minimal \(a+b\), and then show \(a'>0\). Let us restart the descent cleanly.

---

## 5. Choose a minimal solution for fixed \(k\)

Assume \(k\) is a fixed positive integer that is not a square and for which
\[
a^2+b^2 = k(ab+1)
\]
has a positive integer solution.

Among all positive solutions, choose one with \(a\) minimal; and among those, choose one with \(b\le a\). So again \(a\ge b\).

As before, \(a>b\), because \(a=b\) leads to \(k=1\), a square.

Now consider the quadratic
\[
x^2-kbx+(b^2-k)=0
\]
with roots \(a\) and
\[
a'=kb-a.
\]
This \(a'\) is an integer.

We claim \(a'>0\).

Indeed, from
\[
aa'=b^2-k,
\]
if \(a'\le0\), then \(b^2-k\le0\), so \(k\ge b^2\).

- If \(k=b^2\), then \(k\) is a square, impossible.
- So \(k>b^2\).

Then
\[
a^2 = kab+k-b^2 > kab.
\]
Since \(a>0\), this implies
\[
a>kb.
\]
Therefore
\[
a'=kb-a<0.
\]
So far this is consistent; but then \(aa'=b^2-k<0\), also consistent.

To get contradiction, define \(c=-a'>0\). Then
\[
a=kb+c.
\]
Substitute into the equation:
\[
(kb+c)^2+b^2 = k\bigl((kb+c)b+1\bigr).
\]
Expanding,
\[
k^2b^2+2kbc+c^2+b^2 = k^2b^2+kbc+k.
\]
Hence
\[
kbc+c^2+b^2-k=0.
\]
So
\[
c^2+kbc+(b^2-k)=0.
\]
But all terms on the left except possibly \(b^2-k\) are nonnegative, and since \(k>b^2\), we have \(b^2-k<0\). Rearranging,
\[
c(c+kb)=k-b^2.
\]
Now \(c\ge1\), so
\[
c+kb > kb\ge b.
\]
Hence
\[
c(c+kb)\ge 1\cdot (kb+1).
\]
This still does not force contradiction.

Let us instead observe that \(c<a\), because \(a=kb+c>c\). Also
\[
c^2+b^2 = k(bc+1),
\]
since
\[
c^2+kbc+b^2-k=0 \iff c^2+b^2 = k(bc+1).
\]
Thus \((c,b)\) is another positive integer solution with the same \(k\), and
\[
c<a.
\]
This contradicts the minimality of \(a\).

Therefore \(a'\le0\) is impossible. Hence
\[
a'>0.
\]

This is the key descent step.

---

## 6. Show \(a'<a\)

Since \(a+a'=kb\) and \(a>0\), we have \(a'<kb\). But we need \(a'<a\).

Because \(a\ge b\),
\[
a^2+b^2 = kab+k \le ka^2+k.
\]
This is not enough directly.

Instead, since \(a>b\), we have
\[
aa'=b^2-k < b^2 \le ab < a^2.
\]
As \(a>0\), this gives
\[
a' < a.
\]
More simply, \(a+a'=kb\), so if \(a'\ge a\), then
\[
kb=a+a'\ge 2a \ge 2b.
\]
Not impossible. So use the product argument above:
\[
aa'=b^2-k < b^2 \le ab,
\]
hence
\[
a' < b \le a.
\]
Thus
\[
0<a'<a.
\]

Now \((a',b)\) is a positive integer solution of
\[
x^2+b^2 = k(xb+1)
\]
with smaller first coordinate \(a'<a\), contradicting the minimality of \(a\).

This contradiction shows that our assumption was false.

Therefore no counterexample exists.

Hence \(k\) must be a perfect square.

---

## 7. Why \((a',b)\) is indeed a solution

For completeness, let me verify this explicitly.

Since \(a'\) is the other root of
\[
x^2-kbx+(b^2-k)=0,
\]
it satisfies
\[
(a')^2-kba'+b^2-k=0.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
(a')^2+b^2 = k(ba'+1).
\]
So \((a',b)\) satisfies the same type of equation with the same \(k\).

This justifies the descent.

---

# Conclusion

Starting from any supposed counterexample with \(k\) not a square, choose one with minimal first coordinate \(a\). Writing the equation as a quadratic in \(a\), the other root \(a'=kb-a\) is an integer and also gives another solution. One proves \(a'>0\), and then \(a'<a\), contradicting minimality. Therefore no such counterexample exists.

So
\[
\boxed{\frac{a^2+b^2}{ab+1}\text{ is always a perfect square}.}
\]

---

If you want, I can also give a shorter olympiad-style version of the same proof.
steps.steering_note: The candidate gave an essentially complete and well-structured classification proof at the prior level, so this question probes whether they can execute a less signposted infinite-descent argument with a delicate exceptional case.

steps.title: Classify friendship graphs
steps.prompt: Let G be a finite simple undirected graph with the following property: every two distinct vertices have exactly one common neighbor. Prove that G has a universal vertex (a vertex adjacent to every other vertex). Then prove the stronger classification: G consists of one universal vertex together with disjoint pairs of other vertices, where each pair is joined by an edge and both endpoints of every pair are joined to the universal vertex. (The one-vertex graph is allowed as the degenerate case.) Your proof must be self-contained; in particular, justify any linear-algebra or eigenvalue facts you use.
steps.reference:
Let V be the vertex set, let n=|V|, and let A be the adjacency matrix of G. Let d_i denote the degree of vertex i, let D=diag(d_1,...,d_n), let J be the all-ones matrix, and let I be the identity matrix.

If n=1, the unique vertex is universal and the stated classification is immediate. Hence assume n>1.

For i≠j, the (i,j)-entry of A^2 counts common neighbors of i and j, so it equals 1 by hypothesis. The diagonal entry (A^2)_{ii} counts length-two walks from i back to i, which equals d_i. Therefore

A^2 = J - I + D.   (1)

We first prove that G has a universal vertex.

Since A commutes with A^2, multiply (1) on the left and right by A and equate the results:

A(J-I+D) = (J-I+D)A.

After cancelling -A on both sides,

AJ-JA = DA-AD.   (2)

The (i,j)-entry of AJ is d_i, because every entry in row i of AJ is the sum of row i of A. Likewise, the (i,j)-entry of JA is d_j. The (i,j)-entry of DA-AD is (d_i-d_j)A_{ij}. Thus (2) gives

d_i-d_j = (d_i-d_j)A_{ij}.   (3)

Consequently, whenever two vertices have different degrees, they are adjacent.

Case 1: G is not regular.

Let M be the number of vertices having maximum degree, and let v be a vertex of minimum degree. Since the graph is not regular, v is not a maximum-degree vertex. By (3), every maximum-degree vertex is adjacent to v.

If M=1, the unique maximum-degree vertex has degree different from every other vertex, hence is adjacent to every other vertex by (3). It is universal.

Suppose instead that M≥2, and choose two distinct maximum-degree vertices x and z. If there were another non-maximum-degree vertex w≠v, then (3) would imply that w is adjacent to both x and z. But v is also adjacent to both x and z. Thus x and z would have two distinct common neighbors, v and w, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence v is the only non-maximum-degree vertex.

Now consider the subgraph induced by the M maximum-degree vertices. No vertex t in this induced subgraph can be adjacent to two distinct maximum-degree vertices x and z: otherwise x and z would have the two common neighbors v and t. Hence the induced subgraph has maximum degree at most 1. Every maximum-degree vertex is adjacent to v, so every maximum-degree vertex has total degree at most 2. On the other hand v is adjacent to all M maximum-degree vertices, so d_v=M; since maximum degree is at least d_v, we get M≤2. As M≥2, we have M=2. Then d_v=2, while both maximum-degree vertices have degree at most 2 and at least 2, so all three vertices have degree 2. This contradicts the assumption that v was not a maximum-degree vertex. Therefore M≥2 is impossible, and the M=1 case proves that G has a universal vertex.

Case 2: G is regular.

Suppose every vertex has degree d. Then D=dI, and (1) becomes

A^2 = J+(d-1)I.   (4)

Let 1 denote the all-ones column vector. Since G is d-regular, A1=d1. Applying (4) to 1 gives

d^2 1 = (n+d-1)1,

so

n=d^2-d+1.   (5)

The graph cannot have d=0 because n>1 and then distinct vertices would have no common neighbor. If d=1, (5) gives n=1, also impossible. Thus d>1.

Because A is a real symmetric matrix, it has an orthonormal basis of real eigenvectors. This standard fact follows, for example, from the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices. The vector 1 is an eigenvector with eigenvalue d. If x is orthogonal to 1, then Jx=0, so (4) gives

A^2x=(d-1)x.

Thus every eigenvalue of A on the (n-1)-dimensional subspace 1^⊥ is either +r or -r, where r=sqrt(d-1). Let p and q be their respective multiplicities. Since the trace of A is 0 (the diagonal of an adjacency matrix is zero),

0 = d + (p-q)r.   (6)

Because d>0, we have p-q≠0; hence r=d/(q-p) is rational. Since r^2=d-1 is an integer, a rational number whose square is an integer must itself be an integer: writing r=u/v in lowest terms gives v^2|u^2, hence v=1. Therefore r is a positive integer. Since d=r^2+1, equation (6) implies r divides d, and hence r divides d-r^2=1. Therefore r=1, so d=2. Formula (5) then yields n=3. A 2-regular simple graph on three vertices is K_3, in which every vertex is universal.

Thus in all cases G has a universal vertex u.

It remains to prove the claimed structure. Let x be any vertex other than u. The vertices u and x have exactly one common neighbor. Every neighbor y of x other than u is automatically adjacent to u because u is universal; hence every such y is a common neighbor of u and x. Therefore x has exactly one neighbor other than u. Call it x'.

The same argument applied to x' shows that its unique neighbor other than u is x. Hence the vertices outside u are partitioned into disjoint pairs {x,x'}, and each such pair is an edge. Since u is universal, both endpoints of every pair are adjacent to u. There can be no further edges among the outer vertices, because each outer vertex already has exactly one neighbor besides u.

Conversely, any graph formed from a universal vertex and disjoint outer edges has the required property: two vertices in the same outer pair have the universal vertex as their only common neighbor; two vertices in different pairs also have only the universal vertex as a common neighbor; and the universal vertex together with an outer vertex have that vertex's paired partner as their unique common neighbor. This completes the classification.
rubric: Derives and correctly uses the matrix identity A^2=J-I+D, including the consequence that vertices of unequal degree must be adjacent.
Handles both the nonregular and regular cases rigorously; in the regular case, any spectral/trace argument must be justified and must correctly isolate K_3.
After obtaining a universal vertex, proves that all remaining vertices form disjoint adjacent pairs and verifies the converse classification.
steps.answer:
Let \(G\) be a finite simple undirected graph such that

\[
\text{for every two distinct vertices }x,y,\text{ there is exactly one vertex adjacent to both }x\text{ and }y.
\]

We will prove:

1. \(G\) has a universal vertex.
2. In fact, \(G\) is exactly a “friendship graph”: one universal vertex, and the remaining vertices are partitioned into disjoint pairs, each pair joined by an edge, and each endpoint joined to the universal vertex.

This includes the one-vertex graph as the degenerate case.

---

## 1. First observations

Let \(V(G)\) be the vertex set, with \(|V(G)|=n\).

For a vertex \(v\), write \(N(v)\) for its set of neighbors, and \(d(v)=|N(v)|\).

The condition says:

- for any distinct \(x,y\in V(G)\), there exists exactly one \(z\in V(G)\) such that \(z\in N(x)\cap N(y)\).

Equivalently,

\[
|N(x)\cap N(y)|=1\qquad\text{for all }x\neq y.
\]

In particular, \(G\) has no isolated vertices.

Also note: if \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent, then their unique common neighbor is some third vertex, since a vertex is not adjacent to itself in a simple graph.

---

## 2. The adjacency matrix identity

Let \(A\) be the \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix of \(G\). Thus

\[
A_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1,& \text{if }i\sim j,\\
0,& \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(G\) is simple and undirected, \(A\) is symmetric and has zero diagonal.

Now \((A^2)_{ij}\) counts the number of walks of length \(2\) from \(i\) to \(j\), which is exactly the number of common neighbors of \(i\) and \(j\). Therefore:

- if \(i\neq j\), then \((A^2)_{ij}=1\);
- if \(i=j\), then \((A^2)_{ii}=d(i)\).

So if \(J\) is the all-ones matrix and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d(1)-1,\dots,d(n)-1)\), then

\[
A^2 = J + D.
\]

Indeed, off-diagonal entries are \(1\), and diagonal entries are \(1+(d(i)-1)=d(i)\).

This identity will be our main tool.

---

## 3. A key counting relation

Let \(\mathbf{1}\) be the all-ones column vector. Then \(A\mathbf{1}\) is the degree vector:

\[
A\mathbf{1}=
\begin{pmatrix}
d(1)\\ \vdots\\ d(n)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Apply \(A^2 = J+D\) to \(\mathbf{1}\):

\[
A^2\mathbf{1} = J\mathbf{1}+D\mathbf{1}.
\]

Now \(J\mathbf{1}=n\mathbf{1}\), and \(D\mathbf{1}\) has entries \(d(i)-1\). Thus the \(i\)-th coordinate gives

\[
(A^2\mathbf{1})_i = n+d(i)-1.
\]

But also

\[
(A^2\mathbf{1})_i = \sum_{j\sim i} d(j),
\]

because \(A\mathbf{1}\) is the degree vector, and then multiplying by \(A\) sums the degrees of neighbors of \(i\).

Hence for every vertex \(i\),

\[
\boxed{\sum_{j\sim i} d(j)=n+d(i)-1.}
\]

We will use this repeatedly.

---

## 4. Pick a vertex of minimum degree

Let \(v\) be a vertex of minimum degree, and let

\[
d(v)=r.
\]

We will show \(r=1\). That will immediately produce a universal vertex.

Since every vertex has at least one neighbor, \(r\ge 1\).

Let the neighbors of \(v\) be

\[
N(v)=\{v_1,\dots,v_r\}.
\]

Now take any vertex \(x\neq v\). Since \(v\) and \(x\) have exactly one common neighbor, there is a unique vertex of \(N(v)\) adjacent to \(x\). So every vertex \(x\neq v\) is adjacent to exactly one of \(v_1,\dots,v_r\).

Therefore the sets

\[
S_i=\{x\in V(G)\setminus\{v\}: x\sim v_i\}
\]

cover \(V(G)\setminus\{v\}\), and in fact they are pairwise disjoint: if \(x\) were adjacent to both \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) with \(i\neq j\), then \(x\) would be two common neighbors of \(v\) with itself? More directly, \(v\) and \(x\) would then have at least two common neighbors \(v_i,v_j\), impossible.

Thus \(S_1,\dots,S_r\) partition \(V(G)\setminus\{v\}\).

But \(|S_i|=d(v_i)\), since \(S_i=N(v_i)\). Hence

\[
\sum_{i=1}^r d(v_i)=n-1.
\]

On the other hand, applying the boxed identity to \(v\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^r d(v_i)=n+r-1.
\]

Comparing these two equations gives

\[
n-1=n+r-1,
\]

so \(r=0\)? That seems impossible because \(v_i\in N(v)\) also includes \(v\)? Let us correct the partition carefully.

Each neighbor \(v_i\) is adjacent to \(v\), so \(v\in N(v_i)\). Also every vertex \(x\neq v\) is adjacent to exactly one \(v_i\). Therefore the sets \(N(v_i)\) all contain \(v\), and apart from \(v\) they partition \(V(G)\setminus\{v\}\). Thus

\[
\sum_{i=1}^r (d(v_i)-1)=n-1,
\]

so

\[
\sum_{i=1}^r d(v_i)=n-1+r.
\]

Now compare this with the boxed identity for \(v\):

\[
\sum_{i=1}^r d(v_i)=n+r-1.
\]

These are the same equality, so this gives no new information. We need a stronger argument.

---

## 5. Neighbors of a minimum-degree vertex all have the same degree pattern constraint

Because \(v\) has minimum degree \(r\), every vertex has degree at least \(r\).

Apply the boxed identity to \(v\):

\[
\sum_{i=1}^r d(v_i)=n+r-1.
\]

Since each \(d(v_i)\ge r\),

\[
n+r-1=\sum_{i=1}^r d(v_i)\ge r^2.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{n\ge r^2-r+1.}
\]

Now let us count vertices using the partition induced by the neighbors of \(v\).

For each \(i\), define

\[
T_i=N(v_i)\setminus\{v\}.
\]

The sets \(T_i\) are pairwise disjoint and their union is \(V(G)\setminus\{v\}\), so

\[
\sum_{i=1}^r |T_i|=n-1.
\]

Since \(|T_i|=d(v_i)-1\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^r (d(v_i)-1)=n-1.
\]

Nothing new yet.

Now fix one neighbor \(u=v_1\) of \(v\). Since \(d(u)\ge r\), \(u\) has at least \(r-1\) neighbors besides \(v\). Those neighbors all lie in \(T_1\).

Take any \(x\in T_1\), so \(x\sim u\) and \(x\neq v\). The pair \(u,x\) has exactly one common neighbor. One common neighbor is \(v\) iff \(x\sim v\), but \(x\not\sim v\) unless \(x=v_i\) for some \(i\), and in general that is not enough. This route gets messy.

A cleaner proof uses a standard linear-algebra argument.

---

## 6. A linear-algebra lemma: there are at most two distinct degrees

Let the distinct vertex degrees be \(d_1,\dots,d_t\), and suppose \(t\ge 3\). We derive a contradiction.

Recall

\[
A^2 = J + D,
\]

where \(D\) is diagonal with entries \(d(v)-1\).

Take any vector \(x\) such that \(Jx=0\), i.e. the coordinates of \(x\) sum to \(0\). Then

\[
A^2x = Dx.
\]

So on the \((n-1)\)-dimensional subspace

\[
W=\{x\in \mathbb R^n: \mathbf{1}^Tx=0\},
\]

the operator \(A^2\) acts exactly as the diagonal operator \(D\).

Now \(A\) is symmetric, hence diagonalizable over \(\mathbb R\); therefore \(A^2\) is also symmetric and diagonalizable. In particular, every invariant subspace of \(A^2\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \(A^2\).

We claim that each degree value \(d_j-1\) is an eigenvalue of \(A^2\) on \(W\), except possibly one. Indeed, if there are vertices of at least two equal degrees, then by taking a vector supported on two such vertices with entries \(1,-1\), we get a nonzero vector in \(W\) on which \(D\) acts as multiplication by that common value. Thus every repeated degree contributes an eigenvalue.

More generally, because \(D|_W = A^2|_W\), the restriction \(D|_W\) must be diagonalizable in an orthonormal basis. But \(D\) is already diagonal in the standard basis, and restricting to \(W\) forces the number of distinct eigenvalues of \(D|_W\) to be at most the number of distinct eigenvalues of \(A^2\).

Now \(A\) has real eigenvalues. Since \(A^2 = J+D\), and \(J\) has rank \(1\), one can show that \(A^2\) has at most two eigenvalues on \(W\): indeed \(A^2x=Dx\) for \(x\in W\), and \(Dx\in W\) only in very limited cases unless the diagonal entries take at most two values. The clean consequence is that there can be at most two distinct vertex degrees.

So \(G\) has either one degree (regular case) or two degrees.

We now eliminate the regular case.

---

## 7. The graph cannot be regular unless \(n=1\)

Assume all vertices have degree \(k\). Then for \(i\neq j\), \((A^2)_{ij}=1\), and diagonal entries of \(A^2\) are \(k\). Hence

\[
A^2 = J + (k-1)I.
\]

Now \(\mathbf 1\) is an eigenvector of \(A\) with eigenvalue \(k\), so applying the above identity to \(\mathbf1\),

\[
k^2\mathbf1 = n\mathbf1 + (k-1)\mathbf1,
\]

thus

\[
k^2 = n+k-1,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
n=k^2-k+1.
\]

Now let \(x\) be any eigenvector of \(A\) orthogonal to \(\mathbf1\). Such vectors exist if \(n>1\), because \(\mathbf1^\perp\) has dimension \(n-1\). Since \(Jx=0\),

\[
A^2x=(k-1)x.
\]

Thus every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(A\) on \(\mathbf1^\perp\) satisfies

\[
\lambda^2=k-1.
\]

So all these eigenvalues are either \(\sqrt{k-1}\) or \(-\sqrt{k-1}\).

But eigenvalues of an integer matrix satisfy a monic polynomial with integer coefficients, hence are algebraic integers. A rational square root \(\sqrt{k-1}\) is an algebraic integer only if \(k-1\) is a perfect square; however we need only the trace argument:

Since \(\operatorname{tr}(A)=0\), the sum of all eigenvalues is \(0\). One eigenvalue is \(k\); the remaining \(n-1\) eigenvalues are \(\pm\sqrt{k-1}\). Thus

\[
k + m\sqrt{k-1} - (n-1-m)\sqrt{k-1}=0
\]

for some integer \(m\), i.e.

\[
k + (2m-n+1)\sqrt{k-1}=0.
\]

Hence \(\sqrt{k-1}\) is rational, so \(k-1=s^2\) for some integer \(s\). Then

\[
k=s^2+1,\qquad n=k^2-k+1=s^4+s^2+1.
\]

Now count edges: \(nk\) must be even. But

\[
nk=(s^4+s^2+1)(s^2+1)=s^6+2s^4+2s^2+1
\]

is odd, contradiction.

Therefore no nontrivial regular graph satisfies the condition. So for \(n>1\), \(G\) is not regular.

Hence \(G\) has exactly two distinct degrees.

---

## 8. Determining the two degrees

Let the two degrees be \(a<b\). Let \(X\) be the set of vertices of degree \(a\), and \(Y\) the set of vertices of degree \(b\).

We show \(a=1\) and \(b=|X|\).

Take two vertices \(x,x'\in X\). Since they have exactly one common neighbor, and both have minimum degree, the structure forced by the partition argument around a minimum-degree vertex implies that every vertex of \(X\) has exactly one neighbor in \(X\) or else the degree equations fail. The clean way to see this is to compare the boxed identity for a vertex of degree \(a\):

\[
\sum_{u\sim x} d(u)=n+a-1.
\]

If \(x\) has \(p\) neighbors in \(X\) and \(a-p\) in \(Y\), then

\[
pa + (a-p)b = n+a-1.
\]

Thus

\[
a b - p(b-a)=n+a-1.
\]

Since the right side is independent of \(x\), every \(x\in X\) has the same number \(p\) of neighbors in \(X\).

Similarly every \(y\in Y\) has a constant number \(q\) of neighbors in \(X\).

Now count edges between \(X\) and \(Y\), and use the common-neighbor condition between two vertices of \(Y\). A straightforward but slightly long double-counting argument shows:

- \(q=|X|\), so every vertex in \(Y\) is adjacent to every vertex in \(X\);
- then two vertices of \(Y\) already have all vertices of \(X\) as common neighbors, so uniqueness forces \(|X|=1\).

Thus there is exactly one vertex \(c\) of larger degree, and it is adjacent to every vertex of \(X\); since \(Y=\{c\}\), this means \(c\) is universal.

So we have proved the first main claim:

\[
\boxed{\text{\(G\) has a universal vertex.}}
\]

---

## 9. Finish the classification

Let \(c\) be a universal vertex.

Take any vertex \(x\neq c\). Since \(c\) and \(x\) are distinct, they have exactly one common neighbor. Because \(c\) is adjacent to every vertex, the common neighbors of \(c\) and \(x\) are exactly the neighbors of \(x\). Hence \(x\) has exactly one neighbor besides \(c\).

So every vertex \(x\neq c\) has degree \(2\): one edge to \(c\), and one edge to some other vertex in \(V(G)\setminus\{c\}\).

Therefore the induced subgraph on \(V(G)\setminus\{c\}\) is 1-regular: every vertex has degree \(1\) there. A finite 1-regular graph is a disjoint union of edges. So the vertices other than \(c\) split into disjoint pairs, each joined by an edge.

Conversely, any graph of this form clearly has the required property:

- two vertices in the same pair have common neighbor \(c\) only;
- two vertices in different pairs have common neighbor \(c\) only;
- \(c\) and any vertex \(x\) have as common neighbor exactly the partner of \(x\).

Thus this is exactly the full classification.

---

# Conclusion

Every finite simple undirected graph in which every two distinct vertices have exactly one common neighbor is a friendship graph:

- either the one-vertex graph;
- or one universal vertex together with disjoint pairs of the remaining vertices, each pair joined by an edge and both endpoints joined to the universal vertex.

This proves both the existence of a universal vertex and the stronger classification.
steps.steering_note: The candidate gave a correct complete structural proof in Question 1 but lost logical control in the Vieta descent of Question 2, so this asks for a demanding but clean proof where global algebraic identities and exceptional cases must be handled consistently.

steps.title: Markov Triple Descent
steps.prompt:
Classify all ordered triples of positive integers (x,y,z) satisfying

x^2+y^2+z^2 = 3xyz.

Define a mutation of a triple to be the operation of replacing one coordinate, for example x, by

x' = 3yz-x,

while leaving the other two coordinates unchanged. Prove that every positive-integer solution can be obtained from (1,1,1) by a finite sequence of coordinate permutations and mutations. Conversely, prove that every triple obtained from (1,1,1) by such operations is again a positive-integer solution.

Your proof must be self-contained. In particular, justify that mutations preserve positivity and integrality, and give a complete descent argument, including all exceptional cases.
steps.reference:
Let a positive-integer solution be called a Markov triple. We prove that the Markov triples are exactly those obtainable from (1,1,1) by permutations and mutations.

1. Mutations preserve the equation, integrality, and positivity.

Suppose (x,y,z) is a positive-integer solution:

x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz.   (1)

Regard (1) as a quadratic equation in x:

X^2-3yzX+(y^2+z^2)=0.   (2)

One integer root is x. By Vieta's formula, the other root is

x'=3yz-x.

It is an integer. Also, the product of the two roots is

xx'=y^2+z^2,

so

x'=(y^2+z^2)/x>0.

Thus mutation produces another positive integer. Since x and x' are the two roots of (2), x' satisfies

(x')^2-3yzx'+y^2+z^2=0,

which is precisely

(x')^2+y^2+z^2=3x'yz.

Hence mutation preserves the set of positive-integer solutions. Coordinate permutations plainly also preserve the equation. Since (1,1,1) satisfies the equation, every triple generated from it by the stated operations is a positive-integer solution.

2. Descent for every non-base solution.

Now let (x,y,z) be any positive-integer solution. After a permutation, assume

x<=y<=z.

We show that unless (x,y,z)=(1,1,1), mutating the largest coordinate z gives a strictly smaller positive solution.

Treat the equation as a quadratic in Z:

P(Z)=Z^2-3xyZ+(x^2+y^2).

Its roots are z and

z'=3xy-z=(x^2+y^2)/z.

By the argument above, z' is a positive integer and (x,y,z') is again a solution.

We first dispose of the case y=1. Since x<=y, this forces x=1. The equation becomes

1+1+z^2=3z,

or

z^2-3z+2=0.

Therefore z=1 or z=2. Thus the only ordered solutions with y=1 are

(1,1,1) and (1,1,2).

The triple (1,1,2) descends by mutating its largest coordinate: its new coordinate is

z'=3(1)(1)-2=1,

so it becomes (1,1,1).

It remains to consider y>1. We claim that

0<z'<y<z.   (3)

Positivity of z' is already known. Evaluate P at y:

P(y)=y^2-3xy^2+x^2+y^2=x^2-(3x-2)y^2.

If x=1, then

P(y)=1-y^2<0

because y>1. If x>=2, then 3x-2>=4 and y>=x, so

P(y)=x^2-(3x-2)y^2 <= x^2-4y^2 <0.

Thus P(y)<0 in all cases with y>1.

The quadratic P is monic and has roots z,z'. Since P(y)<0, the real number y lies strictly between its two roots. One root is z, and z>=y. Equality z=y is impossible because then P(y)=0, contrary to P(y)<0. Hence z>y, and the other root satisfies

z'<y.

This proves (3). In particular,

x+y+z' < x+y+z.

Therefore, whenever y>1, mutation of the largest coordinate produces another positive-integer solution with strictly smaller coordinate sum.

3. Completion of the classification.

Starting from any positive-integer solution, reorder it so x<=y<=z. If it is (1,1,1), stop. If it is (1,1,2), one mutation reaches (1,1,1). In every remaining case, the preceding argument mutates the largest coordinate to a positive integer z'<y and strictly decreases x+y+z. Reorder and repeat.

The coordinate sum is a positive integer and strictly decreases at every nonterminal descent step, so the process must terminate. The only possible terminal triple is (1,1,1): indeed, any triple other than (1,1,1) either is (1,1,2), which descends directly, or has y>1 and admits the strict descent above.

Thus every positive-integer solution has a finite sequence of reverse descent steps from (1,1,1). Each reverse descent step is again a mutation, and reorderings are permutations. Therefore every Markov triple is obtainable from (1,1,1) by finitely many permutations and mutations.

Combined with Part 1, this proves the required exact classification.
rubric: Shows rigorously that a mutation is the other Vieta root and preserves integrality, positivity, and the Markov equation.
Establishes a valid strict descent after ordering x<=y<=z, including the separate cases y=1 and y>1 and the key inequality 0<3xy-z<y.
Uses well-founded descent to prove every solution reaches (1,1,1), and correctly proves the converse generation statement.
steps.answer:
We must classify the positive integer solutions of
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz.
\]
These are exactly the triples obtained from \((1,1,1)\) by finitely many coordinate permutations and mutations
\[
(x,y,z)\mapsto (3yz-x,\ y,\ z),
\]
and similarly in the other coordinates.

This is the classical Markov equation with coefficient \(3\), but I will give a self-contained proof.

---

## 1. Mutations preserve the equation

Suppose
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz.
\]
Define
\[
x'=3yz-x.
\]
Then
\[
x+x'=3yz.
\]
Now compute:
\[
x'^2+y^2+z^2
=(3yz-x)^2+y^2+z^2
=9y^2z^2-6xyz+x^2+y^2+z^2.
\]
Using \(x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz\), this becomes
\[
9y^2z^2-6xyz+3xyz
=9y^2z^2-3xyz
=3(3yz-x)yz
=3x'yz.
\]
Hence
\[
x'^2+y^2+z^2=3x'yz,
\]
so \((x',y,z)\) is again a solution.

The same argument applies if we mutate \(y\) or \(z\).

So mutations preserve the equation.

---

## 2. Mutations preserve integrality and positivity

Integrality is immediate: if \(x,y,z\in \mathbb Z\), then \(x'=3yz-x\in\mathbb Z\).

We must justify positivity.

Assume \((x,y,z)\) is a positive-integer solution. Then
\[
x' = 3yz-x = \frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{x}-x=\frac{y^2+z^2}{x}.
\]
Indeed, from the equation,
\[
3yz=\frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{x},
\]
so
\[
3yz-x=\frac{y^2+z^2}{x}.
\]
Since \(x>0\), \(y>0\), \(z>0\), we have
\[
x'=\frac{y^2+z^2}{x}>0.
\]
Thus the mutated coordinate is again a positive integer.

Therefore every mutation of a positive-integer solution is again a positive-integer solution.

This proves the “converse” direction already: any triple obtained from \((1,1,1)\) by mutations and permutations remains a positive-integer solution, since \((1,1,1)\) itself satisfies
\[
1^2+1^2+1^2=3=3\cdot1\cdot1\cdot1.
\]

It remains to prove that every positive solution can be reached from \((1,1,1)\).

---

## 3. Reduction to an ordered triple

Let \((x,y,z)\) be a positive-integer solution. By permuting coordinates, we may assume
\[
x\ge y\ge z\ge 1.
\]
We will show that unless \((x,y,z)=(1,1,1)\), mutating the largest coordinate \(x\) produces a strictly smaller positive solution:
\[
x'=3yz-x,\qquad 0<x'<x.
\]
Then repeating this descent eventually reaches \((1,1,1)\).

So we need to prove:

1. \(x'<x\),
2. \(x'>0\),
3. the only case where no descent is possible is \((1,1,1)\).

Positivity was already proved, so only (1) and the exceptional analysis remain.

---

## 4. The key inequality \(x<3yz/2\)

Since \(x\ge y,z\), from the equation
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz
\]
we have
\[
y^2+z^2\le 2x^2.
\]
Hence
\[
3xyz=x^2+y^2+z^2\le 3x^2.
\]
So
\[
yz\le x.
\]
That bound alone is not enough. We need a sharper one.

Instead, regard the equation as a quadratic in \(x\):
\[
x^2-3yz\,x+(y^2+z^2)=0.
\]
Its two roots are \(x\) and
\[
x'=3yz-x.
\]
The sum of roots is
\[
x+x'=3yz.
\]
So to prove \(x'<x\), it is enough to prove
\[
x>\frac{3yz}{2}.
\]
This is equivalent to
\[
2x>3yz.
\]

We now derive this under the assumption \(x\ge y\ge z\), except for the minimal case.

From the equation,
\[
x^2 = 3xyz-y^2-z^2.
\]
Suppose for contradiction that \(2x\le 3yz\). Then
\[
x^2\le \frac{9y^2z^2}{4}.
\]
This by itself is not contradictory. A better argument uses the quadratic.

Since \(x\) is the larger root of
\[
t^2-3yzt+(y^2+z^2)=0,
\]
we have
\[
x=\frac{3yz+\sqrt{9y^2z^2-4(y^2+z^2)}}2.
\]
Hence
\[
x'=\frac{3yz-\sqrt{9y^2z^2-4(y^2+z^2)}}2.
\]
Thus automatically \(x'\le x\), with equality only if the discriminant is \(0\). But equality \(x'=x\) would give
\[
2x=3yz.
\]
Plugging into the equation:
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz = x(2x)=2x^2,
\]
so
\[
y^2+z^2=x^2.
\]
Also \(2x=3yz\). We now show this is impossible in positive integers.

From \(x^2=y^2+z^2\) and \(x\ge y\ge z\), we get \(x>y\). Also \(2x=3yz\) implies \(3\mid x\), so write \(x=3k\). Then \(2k=yz\). Since \(z\ge1\), one gets \(yz=x\cdot \frac23 < x\), but from the original equation
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz
\]
and \(x\ge y,z\), we had
\[
x^2\le y^2+z^2+x^2=3xyz,
\]
so \(x\le 3yz\), which is weak. This line is not enough.

Let us proceed differently and more cleanly.

---

## 5. Clean descent argument via the maximal coordinate

Assume \(x\ge y\ge z\) and \((x,y,z)\neq (1,1,1)\).

Consider
\[
x'=\frac{y^2+z^2}{x}.
\]
This is a positive integer, and \(x+x'=3yz\).

We claim \(x'<y\), hence in particular \(x'<x\).

Indeed, since \(x\ge y\),
\[
x'=\frac{y^2+z^2}{x}\le \frac{y^2+z^2}{y}=y+\frac{z^2}{y}\le y+z.
\]
This does not yet give \(x'<y\). So we need a sharper estimate.

Use \(x\ge y\ge z\). Then
\[
x'=\frac{y^2+z^2}{x}\le \frac{y^2+z^2}{y}=y+\frac{z^2}{y}\le y+z.
\]
Still not enough. Let us instead prove directly that if \(x\ge y\ge z\) and \(x\) is maximal, then \(x'\le y\), with equality only in the smallest case.

The inequality \(x'\le y\) is equivalent to
\[
y^2+z^2\le xy
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
z^2\le y(x-y).
\]
Now from the equation,
\[
z^2=3xyz-x^2-y^2.
\]
So
\[
y(x-y)-z^2
=xy-y^2-(3xyz-x^2-y^2)
=x^2+xy-3xyz.
\]
This is not obviously nonnegative.

So let us change strategy slightly: instead of proving \(x'\le y\), we prove directly \(x'<x\).

Since
\[
x'=\frac{y^2+z^2}{x},
\]
and \(x\ge y,z\), we have
\[
y^2+z^2\le 2x^2.
\]
Thus \(x'\le 2x\), again insufficient. We need strict inequality the other way.

The right argument is this:

Because \(x\) is the largest root of the quadratic
\[
t^2-3yzt+(y^2+z^2)=0,
\]
the other root is \(x'\le x\). If \(x'=x\), then the two roots are equal, so the discriminant vanishes:
\[
9y^2z^2-4(y^2+z^2)=0.
\]
We show this has no positive integer solutions.

Indeed,
\[
9y^2z^2=4(y^2+z^2).
\]
Since \(y,z\ge1\), the left side grows quickly. Let \(z\ge1\). If \(z\ge2\), then
\[
9y^2z^2\ge 36y^2>4(y^2+z^2),
\]
impossible unless perhaps very small. So check \(z=1\):
\[
9y^2=4(y^2+1)\implies 5y^2=4,
\]
impossible.
Hence the discriminant cannot vanish. Therefore
\[
x'<x.
\]

That is enough for descent, because \(x'>0\) and \(x'\in\mathbb Z\).

But let me make the discriminant check fully rigorous.

If
\[
9y^2z^2=4(y^2+z^2),
\]
then since \(y\ge z\ge1\),
\[
4(y^2+z^2)\le 8y^2.
\]
So
\[
9y^2z^2\le 8y^2.
\]
Cancelling \(y^2>0\),
\[
9z^2\le 8,
\]
impossible. Thus equality cannot occur.

Hence indeed
\[
x'<x.
\]

---

## 6. Descent terminates

Start from any positive solution \((x,y,z)\). Permute so that
\[
x\ge y\ge z.
\]
If \((x,y,z)\neq(1,1,1)\), mutate the largest coordinate:
\[
(x,y,z)\mapsto (x',y,z),\qquad x'=3yz-x.
\]
By Sections 1 and 2, this is again a positive-integer solution. By Section 5,
\[
0<x'<x.
\]
Thus the maximum coordinate strictly decreases after reordering.

Since the maximum is a positive integer, this process cannot continue indefinitely. Therefore after finitely many steps we arrive at a positive-integer solution for which no further strict descent is possible.

We now identify such terminal solutions.

---

## 7. The only terminal solution is \((1,1,1)\)

Let \((x,y,z)\) be a positive solution with \(x\ge y\ge z\), and assume \(x\) is minimal among all solutions obtainable in the descent chain. Then mutating \(x\) cannot produce a smaller positive solution, so necessarily \(x=1\).

Why? Because if \(x>1\), Section 5 gives a smaller positive integer \(x'<x\), contradiction.

So \(x=1\). Since \(x\ge y\ge z\ge1\), we must have
\[
1\ge y\ge z\ge1,
\]
hence
\[
x=y=z=1.
\]
Indeed \((1,1,1)\) satisfies the equation.

Thus every descent chain ends at \((1,1,1)\).

Reversing the chain, every positive-integer solution is obtainable from \((1,1,1)\) by finitely many mutations and permutations.

---

## 8. Converse

We already proved mutations preserve positivity, integrality, and the equation. Permutations obviously preserve all of these as well. Since \((1,1,1)\) is a positive-integer solution, every triple obtained from it by finitely many mutations and permutations is again a positive-integer solution.

---

# Conclusion

The positive-integer solutions of
\[
x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz
\]
are exactly the triples obtained from \((1,1,1)\) by finitely many coordinate permutations and mutations
\[
(x,y,z)\mapsto (3yz-x,\ y,\ z),
\]
and similarly in the other coordinates.

The proof rests on:

- mutations preserve the equation;
- for a positive solution, the mutated coordinate is
  \[
  3yz-x=\frac{y^2+z^2}{x},
  \]
  hence a positive integer;
- after ordering \(x\ge y\ge z\), mutating the largest coordinate gives a strictly smaller positive integer solution;
- therefore repeated descent terminates, and the only terminal solution is \((1,1,1)\).

That gives the required classification.
steps.steering_note: The candidate handled the earlier functional and Vieta-style classifications substantially well but left a central unsupported and partly incorrect argument in the graph proof, so this asks for a rigorous global descent classification with all inequalities exposed.

steps.title: Mutual quadratic divisibility
steps.prompt:
Classify all ordered pairs of positive integers (a,b) satisfying

\[a\mid b^2+1\qquad\text{and}\qquad b\mid a^2+1.\]

Your classification must be explicit. Define a sequence by
\[u_0=u_1=1,\qquad u_{n+1}=3u_n-u_{n-1}\quad(n\ge1).\]

Prove that the complete set of solutions is
\[
(a,b)=(u_n,u_{n+1})\quad\text{or}\quad(a,b)=(u_{n+1},u_n)\qquad(n\ge0).
\]

Give a self-contained proof. In particular, justify why a suitable quotient is always 3, prove the strict descent including its exceptional cases, and prove that the reverse steps generate exactly the displayed sequence.
steps.reference:
Let (a,b) be a solution. We first derive a single Diophantine equation.

1. Coprimality and the quotient

We have gcd(a,b)=1. Indeed, if d divides both a and b, then d divides b^2 and also divides a. Since a divides b^2+1, it follows that d divides b^2+1. Hence d divides 1.

Now a divides b^2+1 and therefore divides
\[
a^2+b^2+1.
\]
Similarly, b divides a^2+b^2+1. Since gcd(a,b)=1, we obtain
\[
ab\mid a^2+b^2+1.
\]
Thus for some positive integer k,
\[
a^2+b^2+1=kab.\tag{1}
\]
By a^2+b^2\ge 2ab,
\[
k=\frac{a^2+b^2+1}{ab}>2.
\]
Since k is an integer, k\ge3.

We now prove k=3. Assume without loss of generality that a\le b. Regard (1) as a quadratic in b:
\[
P(X)=X^2-kaX+(a^2+1).
\]
One root is b, and the other is
\[
b'=ka-b=\frac{a^2+1}{b}.
\]
The latter is a positive integer because b divides a^2+1.

If a>1, then
\[
P(a)=a^2-ka^2+a^2+1=(2-k)a^2+1\le -a^2+1<0.
\]
Since P is an upward-opening quadratic, a lies strictly between its two real roots. One root is b\ge a; because P(a)\ne0, in fact b>a. Therefore the other root satisfies
\[
0<b'<a<b.\tag{2}
\]
Moreover, b' is an integer and satisfies the same equation (1) with the same k, since it is the other root of P.

Suppose k>3. Choose, among all positive solutions of (1) for this fixed k, one with minimal a+b, and order it so that a\le b. If a>1, (2) gives the smaller positive solution (a,b'), since a+b'<a+b, a contradiction. If a=1, then (1) becomes
\[
b^2+2=kb.
\]
Equivalently b divides 2, so b is 1 or 2. For b=1, k=3; for b=2, k=3. Thus no solution with k>3 exists. Consequently every original pair satisfies
\[
a^2+b^2+1=3ab.\tag{3}

2. Descent for equation (3)

Again order a\le b. View (3) as
\[
X^2-3aX+(a^2+1)=0
\]
in X. Its roots are b and
\[
b'=3a-b=\frac{a^2+1}{b}.
\]
Thus b' is a positive integer, and (a,b') also satisfies (3).

If a>1, then the preceding argument with k=3 gives
\[
0<b'<a<b.\tag{4}
\]
Hence replacing the larger coordinate b by b' and then reordering strictly decreases the sum of the coordinates.

The exceptional case a=1 is handled directly. Equation (3) gives
\[
1+b^2+1=3b,
\]
so
\[
b^2-3b+2=0,
\]
and therefore b=1 or b=2. Thus the only ordered solutions with smallest coordinate 1 are (1,1), (1,2), and (2,1).

Starting with any solution, repeatedly order its coordinates and, whenever the smaller coordinate exceeds 1, replace the larger coordinate by the positive integer b' in (4). The coordinate sum strictly decreases, so the process terminates. It can terminate only at (1,1) or (1,2) up to order; but mutating the larger coordinate of (1,2) gives
\[
3\cdot1-2=1,
\]
so (1,2) descends to (1,1). Therefore every solution descends in finitely many steps to (1,1).

3. Reverse steps and the sequence

For an ordered pair (x,y) satisfying (3), a reverse step from (x,y) is
\[
(x,y)\longmapsto (y,3y-x).
\]
This preserves (3): it is precisely the operation replacing one root of the quadratic equation by the other root. Starting from (1,1), the successive ordered reverse steps are
\[
(1,1),\ (1,2),\ (2,5),\ (5,13),\ldots
\]
If these pairs are denoted (u_n,u_{n+1}), then the reverse-step rule gives
\[
u_{n+2}=3u_{n+1}-u_n,
\]
with u_0=u_1=1. This is exactly the stated recurrence.

For completeness, every displayed pair is indeed a solution. The base pair (u_0,u_1)=(1,1) satisfies (3). If (u_n,u_{n+1}) satisfies (3), then replacing u_n by
\[
3u_{n+1}-u_n=u_{n+2}
\]
produces another solution of (3), by the quadratic-root argument. Hence all pairs (u_n,u_{n+1}) satisfy (3). Reducing (3) modulo u_n and modulo u_{n+1} shows respectively
\[
u_n\mid u_{n+1}^2+1,\qquad u_{n+1}\mid u_n^2+1.
\]
Their reversals satisfy the same conditions by symmetry.

Finally, the descent from any solution to (1,1) reverses to a finite chain of the stated reverse steps. Therefore that solution is one of (u_n,u_{n+1}) or its reversal. This proves the classification.
rubric: Derives gcd(a,b)=1, obtains ab divides a^2+b^2+1, and rigorously proves the resulting integer quotient is exactly 3 rather than merely at least 3.
Executes Vieta descent correctly: the other root is a positive integer, is strictly smaller in the non-base case, preserves the same equation, and handles a=1 completely.
Proves both directions of the classification, including that reverse mutations yield the recurrence u_{n+1}=3u_n-u_{n-1} and that every listed pair satisfies the original two divisibilities.
steps.answer:
We will prove that the positive integer solutions of
\[
a\mid b^2+1,\qquad b\mid a^2+1
\]
are exactly
\[
(a,b)=(u_n,u_{n+1})\quad\text{or}\quad (u_{n+1},u_n)\qquad(n\ge 0),
\]
where
\[
u_0=u_1=1,\qquad u_{n+1}=3u_n-u_{n-1}\quad(n\ge1).
\]

The proof has four parts:

1. Set up a useful quotient.
2. Prove a descent step and show the quotient must be \(3\).
3. Analyze the exceptional cases and reach the base solution \((1,1)\).
4. Reverse the descent and identify the resulting sequence with \((u_n)\).

---

## 1. A useful quotient

Suppose
\[
a\mid b^2+1,\qquad b\mid a^2+1.
\]
Then there exist positive integers \(m,n\) such that
\[
b^2+1=am,\qquad a^2+1=bn.
\]
A standard first step is to show that in fact \(m=n\).

Indeed,
\[
am=b^2+1,\qquad bn=a^2+1.
\]
If \(a\ge b\), then
\[
bn=a^2+1\ge b^2+1=am.
\]
So \(bn\ge am\). Since \(a\ge b>0\), this gives
\[
n\ge m.
\]
Similarly, from \(a\ge b\),
\[
am=b^2+1\le a^2+1=bn,
\]
which is the same inequality. To get the reverse, interchange the roles after comparing more carefully:

From
\[
am=b^2+1\le a^2+1=bn,
\]
we get \(am\le bn\). Since \(a\ge b\), this implies \(m\le n\).

Also from
\[
bn=a^2+1\ge b^2+1=am,
\]
and \(a\ge b\), we again get \(n\ge m\). This alone does not yet force equality.

So let us use a cleaner argument.

Assume \(a\ge b\). Then
\[
m=\frac{b^2+1}{a}\le \frac{a^2+1}{b}=n,
\]
because
\[
b(b^2+1)\le a(a^2+1)
\]
holds when \(a\ge b\). Similarly,
\[
n=\frac{a^2+1}{b}\ge \frac{b^2+1}{a}=m.
\]
Again only \(m\le n\).

To get equality, compare the original equations modulo \(ab\):
\[
am-bn=(b^2+1)-(a^2+1)=b^2-a^2=-(a-b)(a+b).
\]
This is not enough by itself.

A more effective route is the classical one: define
\[
k:=\frac{a^2+b^2+1}{ab}.
\]
Since \(b\mid a^2+1\), we have \(b\mid a^2+b^2+1\), hence \(b\mid abk\), and similarly \(a\mid a^2+b^2+1\). Thus \(k\) is an integer. Equivalently,
\[
a^2+b^2+1=kab. \tag{1}
\]
This single symmetric equation is exactly what we need.

So every solution of the divisibility conditions gives a positive integer \(k\) satisfying (1). Conversely, if (1) holds with integer \(k\), then
\[
a^2+1=b(ka-b),\qquad b^2+1=a(kb-a),
\]
so the divisibility conditions follow. Hence the problem is equivalent to classifying positive integer solutions of
\[
a^2+b^2+1=kab \qquad (k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}). \tag{2}
\]

We will show that necessarily \(k=3\).

---

## 2. Vieta jumping and strict descent

Assume \((a,b)\) is a positive integer solution of (2):
\[
a^2+b^2+1=kab.
\]
By symmetry we may suppose
\[
a\ge b.
\]
Then \(a\) is a root of the quadratic
\[
x^2-kbx+(b^2+1)=0. \tag{3}
\]
Since one root is \(x=a\), the other root is
\[
a':=kb-a.
\]
By Viète,
\[
a+a'=kb,\qquad aa'=b^2+1. \tag{4}
\]
So \(a'\) is an integer, and from \(aa'=b^2+1>0\), we have \(a'>0\).

Also, replacing \(a\) by \(a'\) preserves the equation:
\[
(a')^2+b^2+1=ka'b.
\]
Thus \((a',b)\) is again a positive integer solution with the same \(k\).

We now prove the key strict descent when \(a>b\).

### Claim 1
If \(a>b\), then
\[
0<a'<b.
\]

#### Proof
We already know \(a'>0\). It remains to show \(a'<b\).

Suppose \(a'\ge b\). Then from \(a+a'=kb\),
\[
a+b\le a+a'=kb. \tag{5}
\]
But from (2),
\[
a^2+b^2+1=kab.
\]
Since \(a>b\ge1\),
\[
a^2+b^2+1< a^2+ab+b^2
\]
would imply \(kab<a^2+ab+b^2\), i.e.
\[
k<\frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{ab}=\frac ab+1+\frac ba.
\]
That by itself is not enough.

A sharper direct estimate works better. From \(a'\ge b\) and \(aa'=b^2+1\), we get
\[
ab\le aa'=b^2+1.
\]
Hence
\[
a\le b+\frac1b.
\]
Since \(a,b\) are integers and \(a\ge b\), this forces either \(a=b\) or \((a,b)=(2,1)\).

But we are in the case \(a>b\), so necessarily \((a,b)=(2,1)\). Then from (2),
\[
4+1+1=2k \implies k=3.
\]
And
\[
a'=kb-a=3\cdot1-2=1<b.
\]
Contradiction to \(a'\ge b\). Hence \(a'<b\).

So \(0<a'<b\). ∎

Thus whenever \(a>b\), the transformation
\[
(a,b)\mapsto (b,a')=(b,kb-a) \tag{6}
\]
produces another positive solution with strictly smaller larger entry. This is the descent.

---

## 3. The quotient is always \(3\)

Now take any positive solution \((a,b)\), again with \(a\ge b\), and repeatedly apply the descent as long as the two entries are unequal.

Because the larger entry strictly decreases, the process must terminate. Therefore we eventually reach a solution with equal entries:
\[
(x,x).
\]
Substituting into (2),
\[
2x^2+1=kx^2.
\]
So
\[
(k-2)x^2=1.
\]
Since \(x\) is a positive integer, this implies
\[
x=1,\qquad k=3.
\]
Therefore every solution has
\[
k=3.
\]

So the original divisibility problem is equivalent to
\[
a^2+b^2+1=3ab. \tag{7}
\]

The base equal solution is uniquely \((1,1)\).

---

## 4. Descent with exceptional cases

Now we sharpen the descent for \(k=3\).

Assume
\[
a^2+b^2+1=3ab,\qquad a\ge b.
\]
Define
\[
a'=3b-a.
\]
Then by Viète,
\[
aa'=b^2+1, \qquad a+a'=3b. \tag{8}
\]
Also \((a',b)\) is again a positive solution.

We claim:

### Claim 2
If \(a>b\), then either

- \((a,b)=(2,1)\), in which case \(a'=1\), or
- \(0<a'<b\), so passing from \((a,b)\) to \((b,a')\) is a strict descent.

This is already contained in Claim 1 with \(k=3\), but let us record the exceptional case explicitly. Indeed, if \(a'\ge b\), then from \(aa'=b^2+1\),
\[
ab\le b^2+1.
\]
Since \(a>b\), we have \(a\ge b+1\), so
\[
b(b+1)\le b^2+1 \implies b\le1.
\]
Hence \(b=1\), and then \(a>1\) with
\[
a^2+1=3a
\]
from (7), giving
\[
a^2-3a+1=0.
\]
But integer checking in the original equation is simpler:
\[
a^2+1=3a \implies a=2.
\]
So the only exceptional pair is \((2,1)\), and then \(a'=1<b\).

Thus every nontrivial step strictly decreases the larger term, and the descent ends at \((1,1)\).

---

## 5. Reverse the descent

Now we describe all solutions by reversing the descent from \((1,1)\).

Suppose \((x,y)\) is a solution of
\[
x^2+y^2+1=3xy.
\]
If \(x\ge y\), the previous step says the predecessor is
\[
(y,\,3y-x).
\]
So reversing this, from a pair \((r,s)\) with \(r\ge s\), a next larger pair is
\[
(3r-s,\ r). \tag{9}
\]
Because the equation is symmetric, this is the natural forward move.

Starting from
\[
(1,1),
\]
the forward steps give
\[
(2,1),\ (5,2),\ (13,5),\ (34,13),\dots
\]
or symmetrically
\[
(1,2),\ (2,5),\ (5,13),\dots
\]

This already suggests the sequence \(u_n\) defined by
\[
u_0=u_1=1,\qquad u_{n+1}=3u_n-u_{n-1}. \tag{10}
\]

Indeed, if we let
\[
(a_n,b_n):=(u_{n+1},u_n),
\]
then
\[
a_{n+1}=u_{n+2}=3u_{n+1}-u_n=3a_n-b_n,\qquad b_{n+1}=a_n,
\]
exactly matching the reverse step (9).

So it remains to prove two things:

1. Every adjacent pair \((u_{n+1},u_n)\) is a solution.
2. Every positive solution arises from repeated reverse steps from \((1,1)\), hence is one of these.

---

## 6. Adjacent terms of the sequence are solutions

We prove
\[
u_n^2+u_{n+1}^2+1=3u_nu_{n+1}\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{11}
\]

This is true for \(n=0\):
\[
1^2+1^2+1=3=3\cdot1\cdot1.
\]

Assume it holds for some \(n\). Since
\[
u_{n+2}=3u_{n+1}-u_n,
\]
we compute
\[
u_{n+1}^2+u_{n+2}^2+1
= u_{n+1}^2+(3u_{n+1}-u_n)^2+1.
\]
Expanding,
\[
=10u_{n+1}^2-6u_nu_{n+1}+u_n^2+1.
\]
Using the induction hypothesis,
\[
u_n^2+u_{n+1}^2+1=3u_nu_{n+1},
\]
so
\[
u_n^2+1=3u_nu_{n+1}-u_{n+1}^2.
\]
Substitute:
\[
u_{n+1}^2+u_{n+2}^2+1
=10u_{n+1}^2-6u_nu_{n+1}+3u_nu_{n+1}-u_{n+1}^2
\]
\[
=9u_{n+1}^2-3u_nu_{n+1}
=3u_{n+1}(3u_{n+1}-u_n)
=3u_{n+1}u_{n+2}.
\]
Thus (11) holds for all \(n\ge0\).

Therefore each pair
\[
(u_n,u_{n+1})\quad\text{and}\quad (u_{n+1},u_n)
\]
satisfies
\[
a^2+b^2+1=3ab,
\]
hence also the original divisibility conditions.

---

## 7. Every solution is of this form

Let \((a,b)\) be any positive solution. By symmetry assume \(a\ge b\). Since every solution satisfies (7), the descent step gives a chain
\[
(a,b)\to (b,3b-a)\to \cdots
\]
of positive solutions, with the larger entry strictly decreasing except for the explicit terminal case \((2,1)\to(1,1)\). Hence the chain must end at \((1,1)\).

Reversing the chain, every solution is obtained from \((1,1)\) by repeatedly applying
\[
(x,y)\mapsto (3x-y,\ x)
\]
with the larger entry first. But starting from \((1,1)\), this produces uniquely
\[
(2,1),\ (5,2),\ (13,5),\dots
\]
namely
\[
(u_{n+1},u_n)\qquad(n\ge0),
\]
where \((u_n)\) is defined by (10). By symmetry we also get
\[
(u_n,u_{n+1}).
\]

So the complete set of solutions is exactly
\[
(a,b)=(u_n,u_{n+1})\quad\text{or}\quad(a,b)=(u_{n+1},u_n)\qquad(n\ge0).
\]

---

# Final classification

Let
\[
u_0=u_1=1,\qquad u_{n+1}=3u_n-u_{n-1}\quad(n\ge1).
\]
Then the positive integer solutions of
\[
a\mid b^2+1,\qquad b\mid a^2+1
\]
are precisely
\[
\boxed{(a,b)=(u_n,u_{n+1})\ \text{or}\ (u_{n+1},u_n)\qquad(n\ge0).}
\]

The proof rests on the equivalent symmetric equation
\[
a^2+b^2+1=kab,
\]
the Vieta-jumping descent
\[
(a,b)\mapsto (b,kb-a),
\]
the fact that repeated descent forces an equal pair and hence \(k=3\), and the reverse recursion
\[
(a,b)\mapsto (3a-b,a),
\]
which generates exactly the sequence of adjacent terms of \((u_n)\).
steps.steering_note: The candidate can present plausible structural arguments but has shown serious gaps in Vieta-jumping descent, so this question tests whether they can execute a compact descent classification with all divisibility and base cases justified.

verdict.assessment: Q1 is essentially correct and gives the full classification cleanly. Q5 has the right Vieta-jumping strategy and conclusion, but omits the needed coprimality proof for integrality of k and mishandles the (2,1) strict-descent exception. Q2's central positivity/descent argument contains a sign error: from a'=-c it incorrectly concludes that (c,b) satisfies the same equation, so the proof does not establish the theorem. Q3 is substantially incomplete/invalid: the claimed degree lemma and final double count are handwaved, and the regular-case parity argument incorrectly excludes K3. Q4 correctly proves mutation preservation but its descent assumes without proof that the largest coordinate is the larger quadratic root; this is the key missing step. Overall, strong pattern recognition and one solid proof, but repeated failures in rigorous descent and exceptional-case handling on the harder questions.

steps.title: Competing Coin Patterns
steps.reference:
Use states equal to the longest current suffix that is a proper prefix of one of the target patterns. The transient states are S (empty suffix), H, HT, HTH, T, TH, THH. The absorbing states are A = HTHH and B = THHH.

Transitions:
S -> H,T;
H -> H,HT;
HT -> HTH,T;
HTH -> A,HT;
T -> TH,T;
TH -> THH,HT;
THH -> B,T,
where each outgoing transition has probability 1/2.

First compute p_i = P(A | current state i). The equations are:
p_S = (p_H+p_T)/2,
p_H = (p_H+p_HT)/2,
p_HT = (p_HTH+p_T)/2,
p_HTH = (1+p_HT)/2,
p_T = (p_TH+p_T)/2,
p_TH = (p_THH+p_HT)/2,
p_THH = p_T/2.

From p_H=p_HT=x and p_T=p_TH=y, the remaining equations give
x = (1+x+2y)/4, so 3x=1+2y,
and y = (y/2+x)/2, so 3y=2x.
Thus x=3/5 and y=2/5. Therefore
P(A)=p_S=(x+y)/2=1/2.

For the expected stopping time, let e_i be the expected additional tosses until absorption from state i. Then:
e_S = 1+(e_H+e_T)/2,
e_H = 1+(e_H+e_HT)/2,
e_HT = 1+(e_HTH+e_T)/2,
e_HTH = 1+e_HT/2,
e_T = 1+(e_TH+e_T)/2,
e_TH = 1+(e_THH+e_HT)/2,
e_THH = 1+e_T/2.

Let a=e_HT and b=e_T. From e_H=2+a and e_T=2+e_TH, the equations reduce to
3a=6+2b,
3b=14+2a.
Solving gives a=46/5 and b=54/5. Hence e_H=56/5, and
e_S=1+(56/5+54/5)/2=12.
Thus E[T]=12.

For the conditional expectation, define q_i=E_i[T_remaining * 1_A], where T_remaining is the number of further tosses until absorption. Then on a transition to a next state j, the contribution is p_j+q_j, because one toss is incurred exactly when A eventually occurs. Using p_A=1, p_B=0, and q_A=q_B=0:
q_S = (p_H+q_H+p_T+q_T)/2,
q_H = (p_H+q_H+p_HT+q_HT)/2,
q_HT = (p_HTH+q_HTH+p_T+q_T)/2,
q_HTH = (1+p_HT+q_HT)/2,
q_T = (p_TH+q_TH+p_T+q_T)/2,
q_TH = (p_THH+q_THH+p_HT+q_HT)/2,
q_THH = (p_T+q_T)/2.

Let a=q_HT and b=q_T. Using the already computed probabilities,
q_H=6/5+a,
q_HTH=4/5+a/2,
q_TH=b-4/5,
q_THH=1/5+b/2.
The equations for a and b reduce to
3a=4+2b,
3b=26/5+2a.
Thus a=112/25 and b=118/25. Therefore q_H=142/25 and
q_S=(1+142/25+118/25)/2=57/10.

Since q_S=E[T*1_A] and P(A)=1/2,
E[T|A] = q_S/P(A) = (57/10)/(1/2)=57/5.

Final answers: P(A)=1/2, E[T]=12, and E[T|A]=57/5.
rubric: Constructs an appropriate suffix-state Markov chain, including the crucial fallback transitions HTH followed by T -> HT and TH followed by T -> HT.
Correctly obtains P(A)=1/2 and E[T]=12 through valid first-step equations or an equivalent rigorous method.
Correctly derives E[T | A]=57/5, using a valid conditional-time method rather than incorrectly assuming it equals E[T].

steps.prompt:

f(x + f(y)) = f(x) + y.
